item.title: Container-Aware Resource Management in Go: The Problem, Go 1.25’s Fix, and What’s Still Missing
item.content:encoded:
If you’ve deployed a Go service to Kubernetes and set careful CPU and memory limits on your pod, there’s a good chance your Go runtime was ignoring them entirely — spawning too many threads, running GC on the wrong schedule, and getting throttled or OOM-killed as a result.

Go 1.25 fixed half of this problem natively. This post explains both halves: what was broken, what’s fixed, what’s still not fixed, and what to do if you can’t upgrade yet.

The problem: Go doesn’t know it’s in a container

When a Go program starts, the runtime reads the host machine’s CPU count and sets GOMAXPROCS — the number of OS threads that can run Go code in parallel — to that number. On a 64-core Kubernetes node, your Go service thinks it has 64 CPUs available, even if your pod’s resource limit is cpu: "2".

The same problem exists for memory. Go’s garbage collector uses a target heap growth ratio (controlled by GOGC) to decide when to trigger collection. By default, it allows the heap to double before collecting. If your container has a 512 MB memory limit and the Go runtime doesn’t know about it, the GC may allow heap growth that pushes your process past the cgroup limit before it triggers a collection. The result: an OOM kill.

These are two distinct problems with different severities.

Problem 1: GOMAXPROCS ignores cgroup CPU limits

What actually happens

Container runtimes use Linux cgroups to enforce CPU limits. A Kubernetes cpu: "2" limit translates into a cgroup CPU bandwidth quota: the container gets 2 CPU-seconds of time per second, spread across all threads.

If GOMAXPROCS is set to 64 (the node’s core count), your Go service creates up to 64 OS threads competing for 2 CPUs worth of time. The kernel enforces the quota by throttling — when the cgroup exhausts its CPU time budget for the current period (typically 100ms), the kernel pauses all threads in the container until the next period begins.

Throttling is brutal. It’s not gentle scheduling slowdown. It’s a hard pause of your entire process. Under this scenario:

  • A p99 latency that should be 10ms can spike to hundreds of milliseconds
  • The Go GC, which runs its own goroutines, can exhaust the CPU budget and cause application threads to stall
  • Context switching overhead multiplies — 64 threads competing for 2 CPUs thrash the scheduler
Node: 64 cores
Pod CPU limit: 2 cores
GOMAXPROCS (before 1.25): 64   ← runtime sees the host
Effective CPU available: 2     ← kernel enforces this
Result: 64 threads, 2 CPUs, aggressive throttling

Real-world benchmarks have shown CPU wait times reaching tens of seconds under this misconfiguration on high-core-count nodes.

The Go 1.25 fix

Go 1.25 makes GOMAXPROCS container-aware by default on Linux. At startup, the runtime reads the cgroup CPU bandwidth limit and sets GOMAXPROCS to the lower of the usual non-container default and the container’s CPU limit. Fractional CPU quotas are rounded up because GOMAXPROCS is an integer.

Node: 64 cores
Pod CPU limit: 2 cores
GOMAXPROCS (Go 1.25): 2   ← runtime reads the cgroup

Two additional behaviors from the official release notes:

Dynamic updates: GOMAXPROCS is now periodically re-evaluated at runtime. If Kubernetes adjusts your pod’s CPU limit on the fly (via VPA or manual edit), the Go runtime will pick up the change automatically — no restart needed.

Opt-out: both behaviors can be disabled via GODEBUG:

# Disable cgroup CPU awareness at startup
GODEBUG=containermaxprocs=0
# Disable periodic GOMAXPROCS updates
GODEBUG=updatemaxprocs=0

Manual override still works: if you set GOMAXPROCS via the environment variable or a runtime.GOMAXPROCS() call, Go 1.25’s automatic behavior is completely disabled. Your explicit value takes precedence.

One edge case worth noting: Go 1.25 respects cpu: limits in Kubernetes but not cpu: requests. The cgroup CPU quota corresponds to the limit, not the request. If you set requests but not limits (a common pattern), Go 1.25’s container awareness has nothing to read and defaults to the host core count.

resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "0.5"    # Go 1.25 ignores this
  limits:
    cpu: "2"      # Go 1.25 reads this ✅

Problem 2: GOMEMLIMIT still doesn’t read cgroup memory limits (not fixed in 1.25)

This is the important accuracy note. Go 1.25 only fixed CPU (GOMAXPROCS). Memory awareness via GOMEMLIMIT is a separate proposal (golang/go issue #75164) that has not yet shipped. As of Go 1.25, GOMEMLIMIT still defaults to “unlimited” — the Go runtime has no built-in mechanism to read the container’s memory limit from cgroups and apply it automatically.

GOMEMLIMIT (introduced in Go 1.19) is a soft memory limit for the Go runtime. When heap usage approaches the limit, the GC becomes more aggressive to stay within it. Without it set to your container’s memory limit, the GC may allow heap growth that triggers the kernel OOM killer before the GC intervenes.

Container memory limit: 512 MB
GOMEMLIMIT default: math.MaxInt64 (unlimited)
Go heap target (GOGC=100): doubles before collecting
If live heap grows past 512 MB: OOM kill before GC triggers
With GOMEMLIMIT=450MB:
GC triggers more aggressively as heap approaches 450 MB
OOM kills become rare

Workaround 1: Set GOMEMLIMIT as an environment variable

The simplest approach. Set it in your Kubernetes deployment to slightly below your memory limit — leaving headroom for non-heap memory (stack space, runtime overhead, cgo memory):

# Kubernetes pod spec
env:
  - name: GOMEMLIMIT
    value: "450MiB"   # 512MB limit minus ~12% headroom
resources:
  limits:
    memory: "512Mi"

Or use the Kubernetes Downward API to derive it from the actual limit:

env:
  - name: GOMEMLIMIT
    valueFrom:
      resourceFieldRef:
        containerName: my-service
        resource: limits.memory
        divisor: "1"   # bytes

Caveat: the Downward API injects the raw memory limit, giving the runtime 0% headroom. For most services this is fine — GOMEMLIMIT is a soft limit; the runtime won’t OOM itself trying to hit it. But memory-mapped files, cgo allocations, and runtime overhead sit outside the Go heap and don’t count against GOMEMLIMIT. Leave 10–15% headroom if your service uses any of these.

Workaround 2: Set GOMEMLIMIT in code at startup

import "runtime/debug"
func main() {
    // Set to 90% of container memory limit
    // Replace with your actual limit or read from env
    const memLimitBytes = 450 * 1024 * 1024 // 450 MB
    debug.SetMemoryLimit(memLimitBytes)
    // ... rest of main
}

This works but hardcodes the value, which is brittle across environments.

Third-party libraries: pre-1.25 CPU fix and memory fix

If you can’t upgrade to Go 1.25, or if you need memory awareness that 1.25 doesn’t provide, two libraries solve these problems cleanly.

uber-go/automaxprocs — CPU (pre-1.25)

The library that Go 1.25 made redundant for most users. A single blank import sets GOMAXPROCS to the container’s CPU limit at startup by reading cgroup v1 and v2 files.

import _ "go.uber.org/automaxprocs"

That’s the entire integration. The init() function runs at startup, reads the cgroup CPU quota, calculates the effective CPU count, and calls runtime.GOMAXPROCS(). If no cgroup limit is found, it leaves GOMAXPROCS at the default.

When to still use it: if you’re on Go 1.24 or earlier. Go 1.25 reads both cgroup v1 and v2, so on Go 1.25+ you’re covered natively regardless of cgroup version.

Migration path: upgrade to Go 1.25 and remove the import. Several major projects have done exactly this.

KimMachineGun/automemlimit — Memory (still relevant on all versions)

Since GOMEMLIMIT container awareness isn’t in Go 1.25, this library fills the gap. It reads the cgroup memory limit and sets GOMEMLIMIT automatically at startup, with configurable headroom.

import _ "github.com/KimMachineGun/automemlimit"

Default behavior: sets GOMEMLIMIT to 90% of the cgroup memory limit, leaving 10% headroom for non-heap allocations. The ratio is configurable:

import "github.com/KimMachineGun/automemlimit/memlimit"
func main() {
    // Set to 85% of container memory limit
    memlimit.SetGoMemLimitWithOpts(
        memlimit.WithRatio(0.85),
        memlimit.WithProvider(memlimit.FromCgroup),
    )
    // ...
}

Supports cgroup v1 and v2. Falls back gracefully if no cgroup limit is found (leaves GOMEMLIMIT unchanged).

tprasadtp/go-autotune — Both CPU and memory, cgroup v2 + Windows

A newer library that handles both GOMAXPROCS and GOMEMLIMIT in a single import, with support for Windows via the Job Objects API in addition to Linux cgroups:

import _ "github.com/tprasadtp/go-autotune"

Constraint: cgroup v2 only on Linux. If you’re on older infrastructure still running cgroup v1 (pre-Kubernetes 1.25, RHEL 8 and below), use automaxprocs + automemlimit instead.

What to use and when

Go 1.25+, Linux, Kubernetes 1.25+ — CPU: built-in. Memory: use automemlimit or set GOMEMLIMIT manually.

Go 1.24 or earlier — CPU: automaxprocs. Memory: automemlimit or the GOMEMLIMIT env var.

Go 1.25+, cgroup v2, need memory automation — CPU: built-in. Memory: automemlimit or go-autotune.

Go 1.25+, want explicit control — CPU: GODEBUG=containermaxprocs=0 plus a manual value. Memory: GOMEMLIMIT env var.

Non-Linux (Windows containers) — CPU: go-autotune. Memory: go-autotune.

Practical Kubernetes setup for a Go 1.25 service

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: my-service
          image: my-service:latest
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "256Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "2"       # Go 1.25 reads this for GOMAXPROCS
              memory: "512Mi"
          env:
            # GOMAXPROCS: handled automatically by Go 1.25
            # GOMEMLIMIT: still needs to leave headroom for non-heap memory
            - name: GOMEMLIMIT
              value: "450MiB"  # 512Mi limit minus roughly 12% headroom

Alternatively, in main.go, use automemlimit instead of setting GOMEMLIMIT manually:

package main
import (
    _ "github.com/KimMachineGun/automemlimit" // sets GOMEMLIMIT to 90% of cgroup limit
)
func main() {
    // GOMAXPROCS handled by Go 1.25 runtime automatically.
    // GOMEMLIMIT handled by automemlimit with its default 10% headroom.
    // ...
}

Summary

The container resource problem in Go has two parts: CPU throttling from a mismatched GOMAXPROCS, and OOM kills from a GC that doesn’t know its memory budget. Go 1.25 solves the CPU side natively and dynamically. The memory side remains a manual step — either via the GOMEMLIMIT environment variable, the Kubernetes Downward API, or automemlimit.

If you’re running Go 1.25 on Kubernetes with CPU limits set, you can remove automaxprocs and get the same behavior for free. For memory, automemlimit remains the cleanest solution until the Go team ships the cgroup memory proposal.

This post is part of a series on Go in production. Previous posts cover goroutine leaks, context propagation, and profiling with pprof. Next: Async Rust vs Go goroutines — the mental model shift.

Container-Aware Resource Management in Go: The Problem, Go 1.25’s Fix, and What’s Still Missing was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Building a Test Health Monitoring Dashboard with Kibana
item.content:encoded:
Our pipelines were flaky for a while. Not dramatically broken, just annoyingly, unpredictably flaky — the kind of flaky where a rerun usually fixes it, so nobody treats it as an emergency. Right up until release week, when suddenly you can’t merge the tickets you need to, because some test nobody trusts decided to fail again.

I wanted something that could tell us, clearly, which tests were actually causing the pain. So I built a Test Health Monitoring Dashboard using Kibana.

In this article, I’ll walk through why I built it, how the data pipeline works, the one technical problem that made this genuinely hard, and what changed for the team after it went live.

The problem

Here’s the thing about flaky tests in a shared pipeline: everyone touches it. Multiple developers and QA engineers start pipelines, rerun failed jobs, retrigger stages — all day, every day. Which sounds fine, until you try to answer a simple question: which tests actually fail the most?

Nobody had a clear picture. Some coworkers started manually collecting flaky tests here and there, noting down “hey, this one failed again,” but it was never consistent enough to reveal the real pain points. We had a feeling something was wrong, but no data to back it up.

I wanted:

  • A single source of truth for test results, across every pipeline run
  • No manual tracking — the data should collect itself
  • A way to see, at a glance, which tests were the actual problem

That’s what got me thinking about how to collect all the pipeline data automatically and aggregate it somewhere central.

How I started

This was 100% my own initiative, done in my own time as a lead/senior developer with a strong interest in quality work. I designed the whole workflow myself: generate a report for every test run, collect those reports centrally, and build aggregations on top of them. Only after I had something working did I show it to my manager.

The plan came together like this:

  1. Every test run generates a JUnit XML report
  2. A Python script runs as an after-script in the pipeline job and parses that report
  3. The script sends the extracted data to Elasticsearch
  4. Kibana visualizes it

Simple on paper. The pipeline job change alone unlocked everything — once test data existed as structured documents in Elasticsearch, building visualizations in Kibana was mostly a matter of asking the right questions of the data.

What the pipeline actually extracts

For each test case, the script pulls out:

  • Test name and class
  • Execution time (in seconds)
  • Status — passed, failed, error, or skipped
  • Branch
  • Test type
  • Timestamp

Each test execution becomes its own document in Elasticsearch. Multiply that by every pipeline run, every day, across the team, and you get a dataset big enough to actually see patterns instead of guessing at them.

The hardest part wasn’t the tech stack

You’d think the hard part would be wiring up Python, Elasticsearch, and Kibana. It wasn’t. The process and the end goal were straightforward the whole time.

The real challenge was developing this using a single Git branch.

When you’re building something that depends on aggregated data — trends, failure rates, “most failing tests” style views — you need enough representative data to actually validate that your visualizations are showing something true. But with everything running on one branch, I didn’t have a clean way to generate that volume and variety of test data while I was still building and iterating on the dashboard itself. I was essentially trying to validate an aggregation pipeline with a data stream that hadn’t stabilized yet.

There was no shortcut around waiting for real data, so I didn’t wait. I generated representative data by hand and pushed fake/mock documents straight into Elasticsearch, just to have enough volume and variety to actually build and validate the visualizations. Once the charts and aggregations looked right against that mock data, I could trust the same visualizations once real pipeline data started replacing it.

The whole thing — script, Elasticsearch indexing, and the Kibana dashboard — took about a week to build, almost entirely because of this data availability problem, not because the individual pieces were hard.

What’s on the dashboard

Once the data started flowing, I built out a set of visualizations, each answering a specific question:

  • Most Failing Test Cases — a horizontal bar chart combining pass/fail/skip counts per test, sorted by how often each one fails. This is the one people actually open first.
  • Test Statuses — a simple pie chart of passed/failed/error/skipped across the selected time range. Good for a quick gut check on overall health.
  • Slowest Test Cases — a table of tests by maximum observed duration, useful for spotting the ones quietly eating your CI time.
  • Count of Test Cases, Sum/Median/Average of Execution Time — the aggregate numbers that tell you how much load the pipeline is actually carrying.
  • Most Skipped Test Cases — because a test that’s always skipped is a coverage gap wearing a disguise.
  • Tests Evolution — a time-series view tracking totals, passes, failures, and skips over time, which is where regressions actually become visible instead of anecdotal.

On top of all that, there are two filters — Test Type (unit, integration, atfw, playwright, nightly) and Branch — so you can narrow the view down to exactly the slice you care about, whether that’s “how’s the nightly suite doing” or “is this feature branch worse than main.”

Did it actually help?

Yes, and pretty quickly.

A coworker got assigned the task of fixing our flaky tests, and she’s now using the dashboard directly for that — instead of relying on scattered notes or memory of “which one failed last time,” she has an actual ranked list to work from.

It also changed what I personally look at. I started digging into our disabled tests using the same data — figuring out which ones are safe to re-enable and which ones should just be deleted, instead of sitting there disabled indefinitely for no clear reason.

Neither of those things were possible before, not because we lacked the will, but because we lacked the visibility.

Final thoughts

This project reinforced something I’ve believed for a while: you don’t need a fancy tool to fix a visibility problem, you need a decent pipeline and somewhere to put the data. JUnit XML, a Python script, Elasticsearch, and Kibana — none of it is exotic. The value came from consistently collecting what was already there and finally being able to look at it as a whole, instead of as scattered, half-remembered incidents.

If your team has flaky tests and nobody can point to which ones are actually the problem, this is a pretty low-effort way to find out. The bottleneck won’t be the tech. It’ll be getting enough real data flowing through a stable enough pipeline to trust what you’re looking at.

References

  • JUnit
  • Elasticsearch
  • Kibana

item.title: Evaluation Is the New Training
item.content:encoded:
The hardest part of building AI systems has quietly moved — and most teams haven’t noticed.

For the first decade of applied machine learning, the game was simple to describe, even when it was hard to win: get labeled data, define a metric, train a model until the number goes up. Evaluation was almost administrative — compute accuracy, F1, AUC, and ship a report. The hard part was the model. Evaluation was the finish line.

That has flipped. And the inversion is more disorienting than most people admit.

What the Old World Looked Like

In classical supervised ML, evaluation was straightforward because the problem itself was structured. You had a label — a ground truth that someone had attached to each data point — and the entire system existed to predict it. “Is this transaction fraudulent?” has a right answer. “Will this customer churn?” has a right answer. You might argue over which metric to optimize or how to handle class imbalance, but the problem's shape was clear.

This meant evaluation had a clean contract: split your data, run inference, compare predictions to labels, and report a number. Do it rigorously, and you know where you stand. The hard problems were on the training side — data quality, feature engineering, hyperparameter tuning search, compute, and generalization. Evaluation surfaced those problems, but wasn’t itself a hard problem.

What Changed

The bottleneck moved when building became easy. Spinning up an LLM-powered system today takes hours, not months. You can have a working prototype of a document Q&A tool, a customer support agent, or a code reviewer by the end of the afternoon. The API handles the model. Prompting handles the “feature engineering.” Infrastructure is largely commoditized.

This is genuinely remarkable — but it created a new gap that the industry hasn’t fully reckoned with.

If you ask most teams building LLM applications how they know their system is working, you get variations of the same answer: they try it. Someone on the team has some queries, sees if the responses look right, and flags obvious failures. This is sometimes called a “vibe check” — and it’s the dominant evaluation methodology in production AI systems right now.

The vibe check is not nothing. Human intuition catches real problems. But it doesn’t scale, it isn’t reproducible, and it has a dangerous blind spot: it catches the failures that look like failures. It misses the ones that look like success.

The Core Problem

Classical ML evaluation worked because the output space was small and the correctness criterion was external. The output a 0 or a 1. An independent source of truth says what the right answer was. The two are compared.

LLM outputs break both of these assumptions simultaneously.

The output space is enormous — a response to a question can be correct, partially correct, technically correct but misleading, hallucinated with high confidence, or correct in content but wrong in tone for the use case. There is no canonical “right answer” to compare against. And the correctness criterion is often internal to the response itself: you have to read and understand the output to evaluate it, which means evaluation requires nearly as much intelligence as generation.

For agents, this problem deepens significantly. A multi-step agent doesn’t just produce one output — it produces a trajectory of decisions, tool calls, and intermediate states before arriving at a final answer. Any step in that chain can fail silently while the downstream output looks plausible. An agent that retrieves the wrong document, reasons incorrectly about it, and then produces a confident-sounding response has failed in a way that a single output evaluation will completely miss.

What Teams Are Actually Doing — and Where It Breaks

A few evaluation patterns have emerged as defaults, each with real limits:

Golden set testing — a curated set of inputs with expected outputs that you run before every deployment. This works until the system changes enough that your golden set goes stale, or until your golden set is small enough that passing it tells you almost nothing about real-world performance. Most golden sets are both.

LLM-as-judge — using a second language model to score the output of the first. This is genuinely useful, especially for measuring coherence, relevance, and style at scale. But LLM judges have their own biases — they prefer longer responses, they’re influenced by format, and they have blind spots that correlate with the blind spots of the model being evaluated. Using an LLM to evaluate an LLM is like asking someone to grade their own exam.

User feedback signals — thumbs up/down, escalation rates, and session abandonment. These are real signals, but they’re lagged, sparse, and indirect. By the time user feedback surfaces a problem, many users have already experienced it.

None of these is wrong. The problem is treating any one of them as sufficient when evaluation now requires a portfolio approach, as training once did.

The Shape of the Solution

What a good evaluation infrastructure actually looks like in this new world is becoming clearer, even if most teams aren’t there yet.

It’s continuous rather than a pre-deployment checkpoint. The system is being evaluated in production all the time, not just before a release — behavioral monitoring that watches the distribution of outputs, flags anomalies, and tracks metrics that matter to the use case rather than generic quality scores.

It’s behavioral rather than output-level. Instead of asking “is this response good?”, it asks “does the system behave correctly across the full range of situations it will encounter?” — including adversarial inputs, edge cases, and the long tail of user queries that never appear in your test set.

It’s multi-layered. Component-level evals for individual tools and retrieval steps, trajectory evals for multi-step agents, end-to-end evals for user outcomes, and red-teaming to actively break the system. These answer different questions, and none of them can substitute for the others.

And critically, it treats evaluation as a product, not a task. Teams that do this well have people whose job is to build evaluation tooling — frameworks, datasets, judges, dashboards — not just to run evals before a release.

What This Means for the People Building These Systems

The mental model shift is this: in classical ML, you built a model and then checked if it worked. In the LLM/agent era, you build a system and then build a second system to tell you if the first one is working — and that second system is often harder to get right.

This is uncomfortable because the first system is the one that looks impressive. Demos are made of outputs, not evaluation harnesses. But the teams that are actually shipping reliable AI products are the ones who’ve figured out that the evaluation infrastructure is the hard part, and invested accordingly.

The question worth sitting with isn’t “does this work?” — it’s “how would I know if it stopped working tomorrow, and would I know before my users did?”

That’s the question classical ML evaluation was never designed to answer. And answering it is where the real work is now.

Where have you landed on this? Are you running systematic evals, or still relying on the vibe check? I’d be curious what’s actually working in practice.

item.title: Reading the Last Written Offset in Kafka – A Producer Checkpoint Pattern
item.content:encoded:
How we used Kafka headers and last offset reads to solve producer restart without outbox pattern or transactions.

Our application was reading messages from a non-Kafka source and publishing them to Kafka.

Everything worked fine. Until the application crashed

We also stored a checkpoint on disk.

That checkpoint told us where to resume after restart.

We were already using an idempotent Kafka producer. So duplicate writes inside Kafka were not the real concern. But crashes exposed a gap. Writing to Kafka and storing the checkpoint were not atomic operations.

Sometimes the message was already written to Kafka… but the checkpoint was not updated yet.

After restart, the producer would read the same messages again.

A classic at-least-once problem. The real challenge was simple:

How do we reliably know where we last stopped?

Our first instinct was to make it transactional

We explored a few options to make these two operations atomic.

  • An outbox pattern.
  • Kafka transactions.

These would have worked. But they also felt expensive. This was just one producer application. We were adding infrastructure to solve a surprisingly small problem.

Did we actually need another system or topic to store the checkpoint?

Then we noticed something obvious

Kafka already had the answer. Every produced message was already sitting in the topic.

And since this producer owned the topic, nobody else was writing to it.

That changed everything. Instead of storing checkpoints somewhere else…

Why not recover them directly from Kafka itself?

The solution had two parts. First, embed the checkpoint value as a header on every message produced to Kafka. Second, on restart, read the last written message from the topic to recover that checkpoint. The first part is simple. The second part is where it gets interesting.

The Implementation

Let us walk through both parts of implementation. The producer side is straightforward. The consumer side — reading the last written message on startup — is more involved.

Part 1 — Embedding checkpoint in header while producing

On the producer side, we added the checkpoint value as a header on every ProducerRecord before sending it to Kafka topic.

ProducerRecord<String, String> record = 
    new ProducerRecord<>(topic, key, value);

record.headers().add(
    "checkpoint",
    String.valueOf(sequenceNumber).getBytes()
);

producer.send(record);

We did not want to change the message payload itself just to carry checkpoint metadata. Hence Headers felt like a cleaner fit.

The business payload stayed untouched. The checkpoint travelled alongside it.

Part 2 — Recovering checkpoint from Kafka on startup

This was the more interesting part. At startup, we needed to answer one question: What was the last successfully produced checkpoint?

At first this sounded easy. Just read the last message from the Kafka topic. Except Kafka does not really expose a direct: “give me the last message” API.

The approach involves three steps: find the last written offset, seek to it, and poll for the message. Simple in concept — but each step has a gotcha worth knowing.

  1. Find the last written offset

We use assign() rather than subscribe() deliberately. With subscribe(), partition assignment is handled asynchronously by the group coordinator — you cannot seek immediately after. With assign(), we take direct control of partitions and can seek right away. Since we know exactly which topic and partitions we want, assign() is the simpler and more appropriate choice here.

//get paritions for the topic
List<PartitionInfo> partitions = consumer.partitionsFor(topic);

List<TopicPartition> topicPartitions = partitions.stream()
    .map(p -> new TopicPartition(topic, p.partition()))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

//We use assign as we need control over partitions and offsets.
consumer.assign(topicPartitions);

//End offset would be lastoffset + 1 
Map<TopicPartition, Long> endOffsets = consumer.endOffsets(topicPartitions);

2. Seek to last offset

Now endOffsets() gives you the next offset to be written, not the last written — so last written offset = endOffset — 1. So will use this to seek.

for (Map.Entry<TopicPartition, Long> entry : endOffsets.entrySet()) {

    long endOffset = entry.getValue();

    // check to avoid empty partition edge case
    if (endOffset > 0) {
        consumer.seek(entry.getKey(), endOffset - 1);
    }
}

3. Poll for the message.

After seeking to the last offsets, we polled the topic

ConsumerRecords<String, String> records =
    ConsumerRecords.empty();

int retries = 0;

while (records.isEmpty() && retries < MAX_RETRIES) {
    records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
    retries++;
}

The retry loop was important. Partition assignment and polling are asynchronous underneath. Sometimes the first poll returned nothing even though messages existed. A small retry loop made startup recovery reliable.

Once we received the records, extracting the checkpoint was straightforward.

for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> record : records) {
    Header header = record.headers().lastHeader("checkpoint");
    if (header != null) {
        long lastCheckpoint = Long.parseLong(new String(header.value()));
        // use this to resume from next sequence number
    }
}

4. Finding max across partitions

If topic has multiple partitions, each partition’s last message may have a different checkpoint value. Take the max sequence across all partitions as the resume point

When NOT to Use This Pattern

This pattern works well in specific conditions. It is worth being explicit about where it breaks down.

  • Multiple producers writing to the same topic — your assumption breaks. Last message may not be yours.
  • High-throughput topics with frequent writes — the “no new messages before startup” assumption becomes risky
  • When partitions are very large — endOffset — 1 seek is fine, but poll retry logic needs to be robust
  • Multi-instance producer deployments — this is designed for single-instance producer.

In the end, this was really a trade-off.

For a single producer with idempotent writes, recovering checkpoint directly from Kafka felt like the right balance.

We did not add another database.
We did not introduce distributed transactions.
We simply reused information Kafka already had.

For our use case, simplicity won.

Interestingly, Kafka consumers solve a very similar recovery problem internally through committed offsets and the __consumer_offsets topic.

I explored that side of Kafka recovery in another article: Kafka Consumer Offsets — Visually Explained

If you found this useful, follow me on Medium for more articles on Kafka, Java, and system design from production experience.

item.title: The Vocabulary of Production AI We Pretend to Understand
item.content:encoded:
Building production AI applications is much more than models. It is about data quality, feedback loops, evaluation, monitoring, governance, and the intentional engineering systems that make intelligence reliable.

If you’ve spent time in meetings where teams are building with models — as an EM, a product lead, a senior engineer who doesn’t live in the ML stack — you’ve probably encountered vocabulary that everyone seems to understand except you.

This post is for those moments.

20 terms that come up constantly in production AI conversations. The ones that actually separate demos from durable systems.

Not-So-Commonly Understood Terms from AI/ML World

1. Feature Engineering

Feature engineering is the process of turning raw data into useful signals for a model.

Think of it this way: a model doesn’t learn from raw data directly. It learns from derived signals. Instead of “here’s a raw log of user clicks,” a feature might be “number of times this user clicked on a product in the last 7 days.” That transformation from raw data to useful signal is feature engineering — and a feature store is where those computed signals live.

2. Feature Store

A feature store is a centralized system for storing, managing, and serving the input signals — called features — that machine learning models need to make predictions.

Beyond reusability, the deeper issue a feature store solves is consistency between training and production. A feature store gives both the training pipeline and the serving system the same source of truth.

A feature store typically has two layers: an offline store (for training, usually a data warehouse or object storage) and an online store (for low-latency serving in production, usually something like Redis).

TLDR: a feature store is what keeps your model’s inputs consistent, reusable, and trustworthy across teams and environments.

Popular Tools in the market:

  • Feast: An incredibly popular open-source feature store.
  • Tecton: A enterprise-grade, fully managed feature platform
  • Cloud Native Options: AWS SageMaker Feature Store, Vertex AI Feature Store (Google Cloud), and Databricks Feature Store.

3. Training/serving skew

Training-serving skew is one of the most common and frustrating traps in machine learning. Put simply, it occurs when the performance of a model during production (serving) does not match its performance during development (training).

Training/serving skew manifests when the data your model was trained on doesn’t match the data it sees in production — and the model quietly suffers for it.

Training-serving skew generally boils down to three main culprits: mathematical divergence, data leakage, and environmental shifts.

The skew lives in the subtle differences between how data is transformed offline versus online — different libraries, different rounding, different handling of nulls, different time windows. This is where feature stores help to keep the data consistent across training and production pipelines, and avoid data leakage (explained next)

4. Data Leakage

Data leakage occurs when information from outside the training data (often from the future or from the test set) leaks into the features used to train a model. In simpler terms, it’s when your model accidentally gets a sneak peek at data it shouldn’t have during training or during inference time, leading to overly optimistic performance and likely catastrophic failure in production.

For example — You want to train a model to predict if a patient has a specific disease. If your training features include a column for Prescription_For_Disease_Medication, the model will quickly learn that anyone taking the medication has the disease. This is called target leakage.

This is one of the most common and deceptive errors in machine learning.

5. Data and Concept drift

When a model’s performance begins to degrade in production because the real world has changed, it is usually due to one of two phenomena: Data Drift or Concept Drift.

Data drift usually refers to changes in the input data distribution, while concept drift refers to changes in the relationship between inputs and outputs (the underlying concept the model is trying to predict).

Data drift happens when the statistical properties of your input data (features) change over time, but the underlying relationship between the inputs and the target remains the same. For example, an image recognition model trained on summer photos might struggle on winter photos.

Concept drift happens when the statistical properties of the target variable change over time. In other words, the meaning of the data has changed, or the “rules of the game” have shifted. For example — The Housing Market Crash**:** Imagine an ML model that predicts house prices based on square footage and number of bedrooms. If the economy hits a massive recession, a 3-bedroom house that was worth $500,000 during training might suddenly be worth $300,000. The input (3 bedrooms) didn’t change, but the concept of what that house is worth radically shifted.

Drift causes models to fail silently and hence it’s important to deploy intentional strategies to mitigate the drift.

Thanks for reading The Fine Tune! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

6. Confusion Matrix

A Confusion Matrix is a simple yet powerful performance measurement tool used in machine learning for classification problems (where the output is a category, like “Spam” or “Not Spam”, “Cat” or “Dog”). A confusion matrix shows where a model is right and where it is wrong.

It is a table layout that allows you to visualize the performance of an algorithm by comparing the Actual values (the ground truth) against the Predicted values generated by your model.

For a binary classification problem (two possible outcomes), a confusion matrix is a 2×2 grid. The matrix is divided into four distinct quadrants:

  • True Positive (TP): You predicted positive, and it was positive. Example: The model predicted a person has Covid-19, and they actually do.
  • True Negative (TN): You predicted negative, and it was negative. Example: The model predicted a person is healthy, and they actually are.
  • False Positive (FP) — Type I Error: You predicted positive, but it was actually negative. Example: The model predicted a person has Covid-19, but they are actually healthy. (A “false alarm”).
  • False Negative (FN) — Type II Error: You predicted negative, but it was actually positive. Example: The model predicted a person is healthy, but they actually have Covid-19. (A dangerous miss).

Instead of just giving you a single accuracy score — which can be incredibly misleading — it breaks down exactly whereyour model is succeeding and how it is failing. It reveals the shape of model failure, not just the overall score.

Next, let’s look at the metrics derived from confusion matrix. These metrics are important because different systems have different trade-offs. Fraud detection may favor recall vs medical systems need more precision.

7. Accuracy

The overall proportion of correct predictions.

8. Precision (Exactness)

Out of all the cases the model predicted as positive, how many were actually positive? You care about precision when the cost of a False Positive is high (e.g., classifying a safe email as spam).

Precision = TP / (TP + FP)

Precision asks, “When the model says something is true, how often is it right?”

9. Recall / Sensitivity (Completeness)

Out of all the actual positive cases, how many did the model manage to find? You care about recall when the cost of a False Negative is catastrophic (e.g., missing a malignant tumor or a fraudulent transaction).

Recall = TP / (TP + FN)

Recall asks, “Of all the true cases, how many did the model find?”

10. F1-Score

The F1-Score is a machine learning metric used to evaluate the performance of a classification model.

The harmonic mean of Precision and Recall. It gives you a single metric that balances both, which is incredibly useful when dealing with imbalanced datasets.

Which is better? More or Less?

More is better. The F1-Score ranges from 0 to 1 (or 0% to 100%). A score of 1represents a perfect model with flawless precision and recall, while a score of 0 means the model is a complete failure.

Here’s a quick cheatsheet

  • Higher is always better (closer to 1.00 or 100%).
  • Use it when you have an imbalanced dataset.
  • Use it when you want a balance between Precision and Recall.
  • If a model has an F1-Score of 0.85 or higher, it is generally considered excellent in most real-world engineering contexts (though this depends heavily on your specific use-case).

11. Feedback Loop

In machine learning, a Feedback Loop occurs when a model’s predictions directly or indirectly influence the new data that will be used to retrain the model in the future.

Essentially, the model begins to train on data that was generated by its own past behavior. If left unchecked, this creates a closed loop where the model reinforces its own biases, preferences, and mistakes over time.

A feedback loop generally follows a four-step cycle:

Example — The Recommendation Filter Bubble (E-commerce & Social Media)

Imagine a video streaming platform. The model recommends 5 sci-fi movies to a user because they watched one sci-fi movie last week. The Loop: Because 80% of their homepage is now sci-fi, the user naturally clicks on another sci-fi movie. The system logs this click and concludes: “Wow, this user absolutely loves sci-fi!” The Result: The model stops recommending comedies or dramas entirely. The user’s taste profile hasn’t actually shrunk; the model’s narrow recommendations forced the user into a “filter bubble.”

Feedback loops can amplify bias, narrow diversity, and entrench bad behavior.

12. Model Threshold

A threshold is the cutoff point where a model prediction score becomes an action.

A fraud model might say: confidence above 0.85? Block. Between 0.60 and 0.85? Send to review. Below 0.60? Let through. The model is the same. Changing the threshold changes your false positive rate, your operational costs, and your user experience.

Threshold decisions are business decisions dressed up as technical ones. It matters because changing the threshold can dramatically change the false positive rate, operational costs, and user experience and associated risks.

13. Batch Inference and Real-Time Inference

In machine learning, once a model is trained, it looks at new data and generate predictions. This process is called inference.

There are two primary ways to deploy a model to handle inference: Batch Inference(offline) and Real-Time Inference(online).

Batch inference is the practice of running predictions on a large group (or “batch”) of data observations all at once, usually on a scheduled basis (e.g., hourly, daily, or weekly).

  • How it works: The data has already been collected and sits in a database or data lake. A scheduled job wakes up, feeds the entire dataset through the ML model, generates predictions for every row, and writes those predictions back to a database.
  • When it’s used: When you don’t need the prediction the exact millisecond a user interacts with your system, or when you are dealing with massive volumes of historical data.
  • Examples — Amazon or Netflix recommendations, Credit Scores

Real-time inference (also called dynamic or online inference) is the practice of generating predictions on the fly, immediately as new data arrives.

  • How it works: The model is deployed behind a web API endpoint (often using tools like Docker, FastAPI, or AWS SageMaker). A client application sends a single request containing input data, the model processes it instantly, and returns the prediction back to the application within milliseconds.
  • When it’s used: When the prediction relies on immediate, contextual data that couldn’t possibly be known ahead of time, and the application requires a split-second response to function.
  • Examples — Fraud detection APIs, ChatGPT

Batch vs. Real-Time: A Quick Comparison

14. Overfitting

Overfitting happens when a model learns the training data too closely and fails to generalize to new data.

It is like memorizing the practice exam instead of learning the subject 🙂

It matters because an overfit model can look excellent in testing but disappoint in production.

15. Underfitting

Underfitting happens when a model is too simple to capture the real patterns in the data.

It performs poorly both during training and in production.

16. Backtesting

Backtesting refers to evaluating a model against historical data to see how it would have performed in the past.

It is common in forecasting, finance, operations, and demand prediction.

It matters because it helps teams test ideas before exposing real users or business processes to model decisions.

17. Model Registry

A model registry is a system for tracking model versions, metadata, approvals, and deployment status.

It helps teams know which model is in production, how it was trained, and whether it has been approved.

It matters because without a registry, model management becomes tribal knowledge and operational risk.

18. Hyperparameters

Hyperparameters are settings chosen before training begins.

They control how the model learns, such as learning rate, tree depth, batch size, or number of training steps.

It matters because small changes in hyperparameters can significantly affect model performance, cost, and stability.

19. Explainability

Explainability is the ability to understand why a model made a certain prediction.

This might mean identifying which features influenced a decision or generating a human-readable explanation.

It matters because trust, debugging, compliance, and user acceptance often depend on understanding the “why.”

20. Champion/Challenger Model

A champion/challenger setup compares the current production model against a new candidate model.

The “champion” is the existing trusted model, while the “challenger” is tested to see if it performs better.

It matters because it creates a disciplined way to improve models without unnecessary risk.

The teams that build durable AI systems will be shaped by people who can ask better questions about the systems around models.

How does the model know it is wrong?
What changes in production?
Could this be data leakage?
Are we monitoring the right signals?
Who is accountable when the system learns from itself?

These questions begin with shared vocabulary. But they lead to something much larger: better judgment.

And in the age of production AI, better judgment may be the most important capability we build.

If this was useful, forward it to someone who’s been nodding along in meetings while quietly Googling

I’m Radhika — building AI experiences and writing about what it’s actually like to do this work from the inside.

item.title: 5 AI Tools Every Siebel Developer Should Know in 2026
item.content:encoded:
Real tools. Real Siebel problems. No hype.

Eleven minutes. That’s how long it took to solve a Property Set bug that had already eaten two hours of my evening, three dead Stack Overflow threads, and one unanswered 2011 forum post. The fix came from a tool I’d been ignoring for months.

The Tool I Did Not Know I Needed

Six months into my Siebel journey, I had a problem that felt embarrassingly simple in hindsight. I needed to loop through a Property Set in eScript, pull specific child records, and push them into an output Integration Component. I knew roughly what I needed to do. I just could not figure out how to actually write it.

I spent two hours googling. I found three Stack Overflow posts, none of which matched my exact situation. I found Oracle documentation so dense it felt like reading legal text. I found a forum post from 2011 with no accepted answer and one reply that simply said: did you check the docs?

Then, almost by accident, I pasted my code into Claude, described what I was trying to do in plain English, and asked for help. The response was specific, correct, and explained why my original approach was failing. Total time from pasting to working code: eleven minutes.

That experience changed how I work. And it made me curious: what other AI tools was I ignoring that could make Siebel development less painful? Over the next few months I tested everything I could find.

This article is the honest list of what actually helped, in the order I would recommend trying them if you are new to Siebel.

The best Siebel developers are not the ones who know every eScript method by heart. They are the ones who know how to find the right answer fast and understand it well enough to adapt it.

Before We Start: Why AI Tools Matter More in Siebel Than Anywhere Else

Most modern development frameworks have excellent online communities. React has thousands of StackOverflow answers. Python has tutorials for every conceivable use case. Node.js has documentation that reads like a conversation.

Siebel does not have this. The community is small. The documentation is old. The forum posts are often unanswered or answered with vague references to a version of the product from 2009. If you are a junior Siebel developer, you spend a lot of time alone with problems that feel unsolvable.

This is exactly why AI tools matter more for Siebel work than for almost any other development environment. They do not replace Siebel-specific experience. But they dramatically reduce the time you spend stuck, confused, and staring at code that will not run.

Tool 1: Claude — Your Midnight Senior Developer

Best for: Debugging eScript, designing workflows, understanding Siebel architecture

I covered this in depth in my previous article, but Claude earns the top spot on this list because it genuinely understands Siebel in a way that no other general-purpose AI tool currently does. When I paste an eScript error and describe the context, Claude does not give me a generic JavaScript answer. It understands what a Property Set is. It knows how Siebel Workflows execute. It can explain the difference between a Business Service method and a Workflow Process step in plain English.

The moment that cemented Claude as my first choice was a production issue I faced at 10 PM on a Thursday. An EAI integration was failing silently, writing empty records to an external system with no obvious error in the logs. I described the behaviour to Claude, pasted the relevant eScript method, and explained what the integration was supposed to do. Within two exchanges, Claude identified that my Property Set iteration was resetting the child pointer on each loop, which is a subtle Siebel-specific behaviour that simply does not exist in standard JavaScript.

That single conversation saved me from spending the entire night chasing the wrong lead.

  • How to start: Go to claude.ai, paste your exact error, paste your code, describe what you expected. Be specific.
  • Free tier: Generous daily usage limit, sufficient for most debugging sessions
  • Pro tip: Tell Claude upfront that you are working in Siebel eScript, not standard JavaScript. This context dramatically improves the quality of responses.
Claude does not just fix your code. It explains why it was broken. After six months of using it, I know Siebel eScript better than I would if I had spent the same time googling.

Check it out: https://medium.com/@eshitanandy/how-i-started-using-ai-as-a-siebel-developer-and-why-ill-never-go-back-1ba64d81ecb3

Tool 2: ChatGPT — The Patient Teacher You Never Had

Best for: Learning Siebel concepts, writing explanations, drafting initial code structures

Where Claude excels at debugging specific code, ChatGPT is excellent at explanation. When I needed to understand Siebel EAI architecture from first principles because no tutorial had made it click for me, I asked ChatGPT to explain it as if I had never seen enterprise integration before.

The analogy it gave me was simple and effective: an inbound web service is like your phone receiving a call from another system, and an outbound web service is like your phone dialling out to one. The Siebel EAI adapter is the phone itself. This two-sentence explanation unlocked two weeks of confused documentation reading for me.

ChatGPT is also useful for drafting initial code structures. If you need to write a new Business Service method and you are not sure how to structure it, describe what the method needs to do and ask ChatGPT for a skeleton. You will still need to adapt it to your specific Siebel environment, but having something to start from is far better than a blank editor.

  • How to start: Ask ChatGPT to explain any Siebel concept using an analogy or real-world example
  • Free tier: GPT-3.5 is free and sufficient for concept explanation
  • Pro tip: Use ChatGPT for understanding and Claude for fixing. They are complementary, not interchangeable.

Tool 3: Postman — The Tool That Made EAI Finally Make Sense

Best for: Testing Siebel EAI web services, debugging integrations, validating SOAP/REST calls

Postman is not strictly an AI tool in the way Claude or ChatGPT are, but its AI-assisted features earned it a place on this list. Postman is a platform for testing APIs, and Siebel EAI integrations are, at their core, APIs. The moment I started using Postman to test my Siebel web services before wiring them into workflows, my EAI debugging time dropped by at least half.

The workflow I use now is simple. Before I configure anything in Siebel Tools, I build the web service call in Postman and test it against the Siebel server directly. I can see the exact XML request being sent, the exact XML response coming back, and precisely where a mapping issue is occurring. This isolates the problem to either the Siebel configuration or the integration logic, which makes debugging far more focused.

Postman recently added AI-assisted features that generate test cases, explain response structures, and suggest fixes for failed calls. For someone new to EAI integration, this is genuinely transformative.

  • How to start: Download Postman free, set up a new request, and point it at your Siebel web service endpoint
  • Free tier: The individual free tier covers everything a Siebel developer needs
  • Pro tip: Save your working Siebel web service calls as a Postman collection. Future-you will thank current-you repeatedly.
Before I used Postman, I was trying to debug EAI issues inside Siebel Tools, which is like trying to diagnose a car problem by listening through the bonnet. Postman lets you look directly at the engine.

Tool 4: Notion AI — The Documentation Tool Nobody Told Me About

Best for: Writing technical documentation, runbooks, meeting notes, and knowledge base articles

One of the most underappreciated parts of a Siebel developer’s job is documentation. Every integration needs a runbook. Every bug fix needs a root cause analysis. Every configuration change needs a change record. Most developers, myself included, find documentation deeply unexciting compared to the actual technical work.

Notion AI changed this for me entirely. I now take rough bullet points immediately after a debugging session, paste them into Notion, and ask Notion AI to convert them into a structured runbook. What used to take forty-five minutes of careful writing now takes five minutes of rough note-taking followed by AI-assisted structuring.

The output requires editing but the hard part, turning scattered thoughts into logical prose, is done for you. For Siebel projects specifically, where documentation requirements are strict and often tied to client deliverables and change management processes, this saves hours every week.

  • How to start: Create a free Notion account, write rough notes about any Siebel task, ask Notion AI to turn them into a structured document.
  • Cost: Notion AI requires a paid plan, currently around $10/month. Worth it if you document regularly.
  • Pro tip: Create a Notion template for your standard Siebel runbook format and ask AI to fill it in each time.

Tool 5: GitHub Copilot — Useful When You Know What to Expect

Best for: Autocompleting repetitive eScript patterns, reducing typing time on boilerplate code

I placed GitHub Copilot last on this list deliberately, because I wrote a whole previous article about why it is not the right primary tool for Siebel development. But that does not mean it has no place in your toolkit. Used correctly and with appropriate expectations, Copilot is genuinely useful for a specific category of Siebel work.

Where Copilot earns its place is in repetitive boilerplate code. Siebel eScript has a lot of it. If you find yourself writing the same Property Set initialisation code, the same error handling structure, or the same loop pattern repeatedly, Copilot will learn your patterns and suggest completions that save real time. It is essentially a fast typist who has been watching you work.

The key is knowing its limits. Do not ask Copilot to debug a complex eScript issue. Do not expect it to understand Siebel Workflow architecture. Use it as an autocomplete assistant, not as an advisor, and it earns its place in your workflow.

  • How to start: Install the GitHub Copilot extension in VS Code. Use it alongside Siebel Tools, not as a replacement.
  • Cost: 30-day free trial, then $10/month or $100/year. Free for students and open source contributors.
  • Pro tip: Use Claude or ChatGPT to understand what your code needs to do first, then let Copilot help you type it faster.

All Five Tools at a Glance

The Honest Takeaway

When I started in Siebel, I thought the path to competence was memorising as many methods, configurations, and architectural patterns as possible. What I actually learned is that the path to competence is knowing how to find and apply the right information at the right moment, faster than the problem can drain your confidence.

These five tools do not replace Siebel knowledge. You still need to understand what a Business Component is, why EAI Adapters behave the way they do, and how Workflow Process steps execute in sequence. But they dramatically compress the time between encountering a problem and resolving it. And in enterprise CRM development, where deadlines are real and senior developers are not always available at 10 PM, that compression is the difference between a stressful career and an interesting one.

Start with Claude. Add ChatGPT for explanation. Bring in Postman when EAI starts mattering. Let Notion AI handle your documentation burden. And once you know what you are doing, let Copilot handle some of the typing.

The five tools in this article are free or nearly free to start. The time they will save you in your first year of Siebel development is worth far more than any subscription cost.

💼 f you found this useful, give it a clap (or 50 — yes, you can clap multiple times! 👏). I write about enterprise tech, AI workflows, and legacy systems from a developer’s perspective. Follow me here on Medium or connect with me on LinkedIn. If you need technical content written for your product or blog, I’m available for freelance projects — reach out!

Read my previous blog on :Building a Voice for India’s Low-Resource Tongues with Neural Machine Translation
Check the upcoming blog on : Everything I spent a year figuring out….

item.title: Retrieval Is Recall. Correctness Is a Loop.
item.content:encoded:
AIAR is a RAG framework that grades every answer against its own evidence, learns from the corrections, and runs entirely on your own hardware.

Retrieval augmented generation is great at retrieval. It can pull the top-k chunks, stuff them in a prompt, and return the completed reasoning. That’s the standard RAG flow, and it works well until it doesn’t.

What happens when RAG generates the incorrect context and the model answers incorrectly (and thinks that it’s correct)? Nothing. Nothing happens.

The same question asked again, will again answer the same wrong answer.

The fix isn’t a better retriever. It’s an emphasis on a closed loop. Grade your answers against the evidence it was supposed to use, catch the contradiction when it happens, and when someone corrects that model, it feeds the correction right back into the system so the next answer is correct. The output becomes the next input, the circuit closes, and the system gets a little less wrong every time you use it.

The output becomes the next input, the circuit closes, and the system gets a little less wrong every time you use it.

That loop can be found entirely in the open-source framework “AIAR”. It can run entirely on your own hardware, against your own Ollama instance, with no cloud needed anywhere.

AIAR

AIAR (Artificial Intelligence & RAG). A local first, RAG framework built with Python. It can run against your own Ollama instance, ingest your own documents, and it ships three production-grade features that most stacks leave out.

  • Hybrid retrieval — lexical and semantic, fused, optionally reranked.
  • An LLM-as-judge that returns a structured Verdict on every answer.
  • A grounding loop that takes accepted corrections and feeds them back into future answers — so the same mistake doesn’t happen twice.

Calls to the cloud? Not needed. Telemetry? Nope. Vendor lock-in? Don’t think so.

You can run the entire AIAR framework to a Qwen-class model and outpace frontier models in that context. The best part? You can audit every single byte that the models see, use, and return.

Installing it is one line:

pip install 'aiar-rag[rag]'

(The PyPI distribution is aiar-rag because aiar was already taken — but you still import aiar in code. Small naming tax, paid in full.)

You’ll need Python 3.10+ and a running Ollama daemon with at least one chat model and one embedding model pulled:

ollama pull qwen2.5:7b
ollama pull nomic-embed-text

That’s it. What’s the difference?

RAG is a pipeline. AIAR is a loop.

RAG: A question comes in, embeddings and a prompt happen, and an answer comes out the other end. Then it’s gone. Was it good? Was it right? Was it wrong? Could it have been better?

AIAR shapes that flow into a circle. The answer doesn’t fall off the end, it flows into a judge that grades it against evidence. Then, the grade (whether by LLM or human) flows into a grounding store and that store flows back into the front of the system. The end becomes the beginning.

The payoffs compound. Eventually you have a finely grounded RAG pipeline using a closed loop. New context enters and the grounding is reshaped against it.

The 60-Second Demo

from aiar.harness.pipeline import answer_prompt

result = answer_prompt(
    "What did our Q3 deployment doc say about rollback?",
    judge=True,
)

print(result["answer"])
print(result["verdict"])
# {"rating": "good" | "partial" | "bad",
#  "reason": "...names the specific error or why it's right...",
#  "failure_tags": ["hallucinated_fact", "contradicts_context", ...],
#  "confidence": "low" | "medium" | "high"}

That result carries not only the answer, but it tells you whether the answerer actually got the grounded context, whether a past correction was re-injected, which retrieval features were live for this call, the latency, and a call id to trace and audit the entire flow later. The answer moves from being a single data point, to an entire metadata answer.

Evidence comes in (retrieval), a graded verdict comes out (judge), and the accepted corrections circle back to the front (grounding).

Three stages:
Retrieval that doesn’t make you choose:
-Vector search can find things that roughly mean the same. Keyword search can find the same terms in a chunk. Most frameworks pick one. AIAR runs both and merges the results. A question about a specific part number and a question about a fuzzy concept both land at the right chunk.

A judge that sees what you saw:
-From confident liar to truthful. Turn the judge (human or LLM judge) on and every answer gets graded by a second model of your choice. Good, partial, or bad. Along with a reason that names the specific error. With a structured verdict, the code can continuously act and react on it. It’s a checkpoint you can build on continuously.

Contiuation of the loop:
-Catching a hallucination once is a worry. Catching it, fixing it, and never seeing it again is a solution. When a verdict is accepted (by you, a team member, an automation, or another LLM), AIAR saves the correction. The next time that same or similar question comes, the grounding corrections insert themselves in the front before the model answers. The model walks in holding the context, the correction, and essentially the answer.

ingest → retrieve → answer → judge → evaluate → reground ↩

The loop is the pitch. What makes AIAR usable for real work is the plumbing around it:

  • Multiple corpora, kept separate — run a tax corpus, a finance corpus, and a support corpus side by side, each with its own documents and its own corrections, with no cross-contamination.
  • CLI first, HTTP optional — drive everything from the command line, or stand up a small web service if another app needs to call in.
  • A review GUI — a local console to run a prompt, see the verdict, score it, and reground, and to switch models and corpora live without a restart.
  • A preflight check — aiar-doctor tells you in one command whether your Python, your dependencies, and your Ollama install are actually ready, so "it doesn't work" becomes a specific, fixable line.

AIAR is built for your own machine or a trusted network, not as a hardened public service. If you need to reach it from elsewhere, put it behind a VPN or an SSH tunnel.

Try it

If you’ve ever watched a local RAG demo confidently invent a fact and thought “there has to be a layer that catches this”..

pip install 'aiar-rag[rag]'

The repo lives at github.com/wiggins-j/aiar, the PLAYBOOK.md walks you from "pull a model" all the way through "verify the regrounded answer improved" with real, copy-paste commands, and the examples/feature-guides/ folder has a short runnable guide for every retrieval knob.

Pull a model. Ingest your own documents. Ask it something hard. And when it gets something wrong, watch the loop catch it and correct it, so it stays caught.

It’s Apache-2.0. Go own your stack.
